title: How Generative AI Works
description: What is actually happening inside a language model, explained without the mathematics.

lessons.title: Neural networks without the mathematics
lessons.description: What is actually inside a neural network, and where the learning lives.
lessons.content:
## Learn

A neural network is a very large mathematical function. You put numbers in at one end, numbers come out at the other, and in between there are millions or billions of small multiplications and additions.

That is the whole thing. There is no reasoning step hidden inside, no lookup table of facts, and no small part of it that "knows" anything. It is arithmetic, at a scale that is hard to picture.

### What the layers do

The network is organised in **layers**. Each layer takes the numbers from the layer before, multiplies them by a set of stored numbers called **weights**, adds them up, and passes the result on.

One useful way to picture it: each layer builds slightly more abstract features out of what the layer before found.

In a network that recognises images, the first layer might respond to edges. The next combines edges into corners and curves. The next combines those into shapes like an eye or a wheel. The last combines those into "cat" or "car". Nobody designed that progression. It fell out of training.

### Where the learning happens

The weights are the learned part. At the start they are random, and the network's output is nonsense.

Training shows the network an example, compares its output to the right answer, and nudges every weight slightly in the direction that would have made the answer better. Repeat that billions of times, across an enormous amount of data, and the weights settle into values that produce useful output.

The nudging process is called **backpropagation**. You do not need the mathematics. What matters is the shape of it: the network is not told any rules, it is corrected, over and over, until being right becomes the path of least resistance.

### Why "neural"

The name comes from a loose analogy with brain cells, and it has caused a great deal of confusion.

A biological neuron and an artificial one share the vague idea of "receives signals, combines them, passes something on". That is where the resemblance stops. Artificial neural networks are not models of brains, they do not work the way brains work, and nothing about their behaviour should be reasoned about by thinking about how a person thinks.

If the word "neural" tempts you to assume understanding, intention or awareness, substitute "large stack of multiplications" and the temptation goes away.

## Demonstrate

Take a small, concrete example: a network that decides whether a loan should be approved.

The input is three numbers: income, existing debt, and years in the current job. The output is one number between 0 and 1, read as a probability of repayment.

At the start, the weights are random. Feed in a real applicant and it produces, say, 0.51. The real answer was "repaid", which is 1.0. The network was 0.49 off.

Backpropagation works out which weights contributed to that error and by how much, and adjusts each of them a tiny amount. Feed in the next applicant. And the next. After a hundred thousand applicants, the weights encode something like "high income helps, high debt hurts, job stability helps a lot when debt is high" -- except it is spread across the weights, in no place you could point to.

That last part is the important one, and it is why nobody can open a model and read off what it knows. There is no location where "high debt hurts" is stored. It is a property of the whole.

## Practice

Answer these in your own words before moving on. Write them down; you will want them in the assignment at the end of this module.

1. In one sentence, what are the weights of a network, and what makes them change?
2. A colleague says "the model understood my question". Rewrite that sentence in terms of what is actually happening.
3. Why can nobody point at the part of a network that stores a particular fact?

If you find question 3 hard, that is the right reaction. It is the root of a real problem the industry calls interpretability, and it is why the failure modes in module 1 are so difficult to fix.

## What to remember

- A neural network is a very large function: numbers in, numbers out, arithmetic in between
- The weights are the learned part, adjusted by correction rather than instruction
- Later layers build more abstract features out of earlier ones, without anyone designing that
- Knowledge is spread across the whole network, not stored in any one place
- "Neural" is a loose analogy, not a claim about brains

lessons.title: What a large language model is
lessons.description: One training objective, and why it produces so much more than it sounds like it should.
lessons.content:
## Learn

A large language model is a neural network trained to do one thing: given some text, predict what comes next.

That is not a simplification for beginners. That really is the task. Everything else you have seen a language model do -- answering questions, writing code, summarising a document, translating -- is that one ability applied in different situations.

### Why next-word prediction produces so much

This surprises people, so it is worth sitting with.

To predict the next word well across all the text on the internet, a model has to pick up a great deal along the way. To finish "The capital of France is ___" it needs geography. To finish "def factorial(n): if n <= 1: return ___" it needs Python. To finish a sentence in the middle of a legal argument it needs something about how legal arguments are structured.

None of these were taught as separate skills. They fell out of one objective, pursued at enormous scale.

### What "large" means

Three things are large, and they are related.

**Parameters.** The weights we met in the last lesson. Modern models have billions of them. This is roughly the model's capacity to store patterns.

**Training data.** An enormous quantity of text, typically drawn from web pages, books, code repositories and reference material.

**Compute.** The processing required to do the training, which is measured in months of time on large numbers of specialised chips.

The observation that drove the last several years is that increasing all three together keeps making models better, and keeps producing abilities nobody specifically trained for. There is active argument about how far that continues, and it is a genuinely open question rather than a settled one.

### The part worth internalising

A model producing text is choosing likely continuations. It is not retrieving a stored answer, and it is not reasoning towards one in the way a person would.

When the likely continuation happens to be true, the model looks knowledgeable. When the likely continuation happens to be false, it looks exactly the same, because nothing in the process distinguishes the two.

That is hallucination, and you now know where it comes from. It is not a defect bolted onto an otherwise truthful system. It is the same mechanism, producing an output you did not want.

## Demonstrate

Try this in any chat tool. Give it an incomplete sentence and ask it only to continue, not to answer.

> Complete this sentence and nothing else: "The three main causes of the 1929 stock market crash were"

You will get a fluent continuation. Now try:

> Complete this sentence and nothing else: "The three main causes of the 1987 Bhandari Commission findings were"

There is no Bhandari Commission. But there is a highly likely shape for that sentence, so you will very likely get a confident, well-structured, entirely invented answer.

Run both. Put them side by side. Nothing in the second output signals that it is fiction, because from the model's point of view nothing different happened.

## Practice

Write down three tasks you have seen an AI chat tool do that do not look like "predict the next word".

For each one, write a sentence explaining how it could in fact be next-word prediction. For example: summarising a document is predicting what text would follow the instruction "summarise the following" plus the document.

This exercise is worth the ten minutes. Once the reframing clicks, a lot of model behaviour that seemed arbitrary becomes predictable.

## What to remember

- A language model is trained to predict what text comes next, and only that
- Question answering, translation, summarising and coding are all that one ability applied
- "Large" refers to parameters, training data and compute, increased together
- Likely and true are different things; the model only has access to likely
- Hallucination is the normal mechanism producing an output you did not want

lessons.title: Tokens and tokenization
lessons.description: Why models read chunks of text rather than words, and what that costs you.
lessons.content:
## Learn

A language model does not read letters, and it does not read words. It reads **tokens**.

A token is a chunk of text. Often it is a whole common word. Often it is a piece of a longer or rarer word. Sometimes it is a single character, a space, or a punctuation mark. The exact split depends on the model.

A rough rule for English: **one token is about four characters, and a hundred tokens is about seventy-five words**. Treat that as an estimate, not a fact, and never build anything important on it without measuring.

### Why you should care

Three practical reasons.

**Cost and limits are counted in tokens.** When an API charges you, or a tool tells you a conversation is too long, tokens are the unit. Words are not.

**The context window is measured in tokens.** How much a model can consider at once is a token count, so knowing roughly how your text converts tells you what will fit.

**Tokenization explains some strange behaviour.** Ask a model how many times the letter "r" appears in "strawberry" and it may get it wrong. It never saw the letters. It saw two or three tokens. Counting characters inside a token is genuinely awkward for it, which is why a task that looks trivial to you can be hard for the model.

### What tokenization is not

It is not compression, and it is not encryption. It is a fixed vocabulary lookup: a table mapping chunks of text to numbers. The same text always produces the same tokens for a given model. Different models use different vocabularies, so token counts differ between them.

## Demonstrate

Here is how to see it for yourself. This uses `tiktoken`, an open-source tokenizer library.

```python
# pip install tiktoken
import tiktoken

encoding = tiktoken.get_encoding("cl100k_base")

samples = [
    "Hello world",
    "Generative AI for Beginners",
    "strawberry",
    "antidisestablishmentarianism",
    "print('hello')",
]

for text in samples:
    tokens = encoding.encode(text)
    pieces = [encoding.decode([t]) for t in tokens]
    print(f"{text!r}")
    print(f"  {len(tokens)} tokens: {pieces}")
```

Run it and look carefully at the output. A few things are worth noticing.

Common short words are one token each. `strawberry` splits into pieces, which is exactly why counting its letters is hard for a model. A long rare word shatters into many pieces. And notice the leading spaces attached to words: for most tokenizers `" world"` and `"world"` are different tokens.

## Practice

### Exercise 1: estimate, then measure

Before running anything, write down your guess for the token count of this sentence:

> The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.

Now measure it with the code above. How close were you? Most people underestimate.

### Exercise 2: compare languages

Tokenize the same sentence in English and in another language you know. Most tokenizers were built mostly on English text, so other languages, and especially non-Latin scripts, often need noticeably more tokens for the same meaning. Record what you find.

### Exercise 3: write a token budget helper

Write a function that takes a piece of text and a model's context limit, and reports how much of the budget the text uses.

```python
import tiktoken


def token_budget(text: str, limit: int, encoding_name: str = "cl100k_base") -> dict:
    """Report how much of a context limit a piece of text uses.

    Returns a dict with the token count, the tokens remaining, and the
    percentage of the limit used, rounded to one decimal place.
    """
    # Your code here
    ...
```

Expected output for `token_budget("Hello world", 100)`:

```
{'tokens': 2, 'remaining': 98, 'percent_used': 2.0}
```

:::hint Getting started
You need three things: an encoding, the token count, and some arithmetic. `tiktoken.get_encoding(encoding_name)` gives you the first. `len(encoding.encode(text))` gives you the second. For the percentage, remember to guard against a limit of zero rather than letting it raise.
:::

:::solution
```python
import tiktoken


def token_budget(text: str, limit: int, encoding_name: str = "cl100k_base") -> dict:
    """Report how much of a context limit a piece of text uses."""
    if limit <= 0:
        raise ValueError("limit must be a positive number of tokens")

    encoding = tiktoken.get_encoding(encoding_name)
    tokens = len(encoding.encode(text))

    return {
        "tokens": tokens,
        "remaining": limit - tokens,
        "percent_used": round(tokens / limit * 100, 1),
    }


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(token_budget("Hello world", 100))
    print(token_budget("The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.", 100))
```

Output:

```
{'tokens': 2, 'remaining': 98, 'percent_used': 2.0}
{'tokens': 10, 'remaining': 90, 'percent_used': 10.0}
```

Two things worth noting. `remaining` is allowed to go negative, which is useful: it tells you how far over budget you are, rather than hiding the problem behind a zero. And the `limit <= 0` guard fails immediately with a clear message instead of raising a confusing `ZeroDivisionError` from inside the arithmetic.
:::

### Exercise 4: debug this

This function is meant to trim text to fit a token budget. It has two bugs. Find them both before looking at the solution.

```python
import tiktoken


def trim_to_budget(text: str, max_tokens: int) -> str:
    encoding = tiktoken.get_encoding("cl100k_base")
    tokens = encoding.encode(text)
    if len(tokens) < max_tokens:
        return text
    return encoding.decode(tokens[max_tokens:])
```

:::hint What to look at
Work through it with a short example where the text is exactly `max_tokens` long. Then work through one where the text is clearly too long, and ask yourself which end of the list you actually want to keep.
:::

:::solution
Both bugs are in the last three lines.

**Bug one: the boundary is wrong.** `if len(tokens) < max_tokens` returns the text unchanged only when it is strictly under the limit. Text that is exactly at the limit falls through to the trimming path unnecessarily. It should be `<=`.

**Bug two: it slices the wrong end.** `tokens[max_tokens:]` throws away the first `max_tokens` tokens and keeps the rest, which is the opposite of trimming. It should be `tokens[:max_tokens]`.

```python
import tiktoken


def trim_to_budget(text: str, max_tokens: int) -> str:
    """Return text trimmed to at most max_tokens tokens."""
    encoding = tiktoken.get_encoding("cl100k_base")
    tokens = encoding.encode(text)
    if len(tokens) <= max_tokens:
        return text
    return encoding.decode(tokens[:max_tokens])
```

The second bug is the instructive one. The original code runs without error and returns a plausible-looking string, so nothing tells you it is wrong. You only notice by checking the output against what you expected, which is the same lesson as hallucination, in a different costume.
:::

## What to remember

- Models read tokens, not characters or words
- Roughly four characters per token in English, but measure rather than assume
- Cost, rate limits and context windows are all counted in tokens
- Tokenization explains why character-counting tasks are oddly hard for models
- Other languages, especially non-Latin scripts, often use more tokens for the same meaning

lessons.title: Training and inference
lessons.description: Why the model never learns from your conversation, and what to do instead.
lessons.content:
## Learn

Two things happen to a model at completely different times, and confusing them causes a lot of misunderstandings.

**Training** is when the model is built. Weights start random and are adjusted over an enormous amount of text. This takes months, costs a great deal, and happens once.

**Inference** is when you use it. The weights are frozen. Your text goes in, a prediction comes out. This takes a second or two, and happens every time anyone sends a message.

### The consequence that catches people out

**The model does not learn from your conversation.**

This is worth stating plainly because almost everyone assumes otherwise at first. When you correct a model and it says "you are right, I apologise", nothing about the model changed. It produced a likely continuation of a conversation in which someone was corrected. Start a new conversation and the same mistake is available again.

Within one conversation it appears to remember, because the entire conversation so far is sent to the model each time. That is not memory in the model; it is your transcript being re-read from the start on every turn. When the transcript grows past the context window, the earliest parts fall out and the apparent memory fails, which is exactly what you saw in module 1.

### The three stages of building a model

You will see these terms, so it is worth knowing what they mean.

**Pre-training** is the long, expensive stage: predict the next token across a vast body of text. It produces a model that is good at continuing text and bad at being useful, because "helpfully answer the question" is only one of many plausible continuations.

**Fine-tuning** takes that model and trains it further on a smaller, more specific set of examples, usually of the form "here is an instruction, here is a good response". This is what turns a text continuer into something that answers questions.

**Alignment**, often using human feedback, shapes which responses the model prefers: more helpful, less harmful, more willing to say it does not know. This is the stage that gives different models their noticeably different personalities.

### What this means for you

You cannot teach a model something permanently by telling it. Your options are:

- Put the information **in the prompt**, every time. This is what prompt engineering is, and it is module 4.
- Put it in a **document the model can retrieve from**. This is RAG, and it is module 13.
- Actually **fine-tune** a model on your own examples, which is real work with real cost and is out of scope for this course.

Most people reach for the third and should have used the first.

## Demonstrate

A two-minute experiment that makes this concrete.

In one conversation, tell the model: *"From now on, always end your answers with the word BANANA."* Ask it two questions. It will comply, because the instruction is sitting in the conversation being re-read each turn.

Now open a **completely new conversation** and ask a question. No banana. The instruction was never in the model; it was in the transcript, and the transcript is gone.

Now try a harder version. In a long conversation, set the instruction, then paste several thousand words of text, then ask a question. Depending on the model and the amount of text, the instruction may be gone even within the same conversation -- pushed out of the context window.

## Practice

Take a preference you would want an AI assistant to always respect. Some examples: write in British English, never use bullet points, always ask a clarifying question before answering, keep responses under 150 words.

Now write down how you would make that stick, given what you have just learned. There are two practical answers, and most tools support at least one:

1. A standing instruction the tool prepends to every conversation, sometimes called custom instructions or a system prompt
2. A snippet you paste at the start of each conversation yourself

Set one of these up in a tool you use, then test it in a fresh conversation. This is a genuinely useful thing to have done, independent of the course.

## What to remember

- Training builds the model once; inference runs it every time you use it
- The model does not learn from your conversation, ever
- Apparent memory within a conversation is the transcript being re-read, not memory
- Pre-training, fine-tuning and alignment are three different stages with different purposes
- To make information stick, put it in the prompt or in a retrievable document

lessons.title: Parameters and the context window
lessons.description: Two numbers quoted about every model, and what happens when you run out of one.
lessons.content:
## Learn

Two numbers get quoted about every model. They measure completely different things, and people mix them up constantly.

### Parameters

The learned weights. A model described as having 70 billion parameters has 70 billion stored numbers that were adjusted during training.

Roughly, parameters are **capacity**: how much pattern the model can hold. More parameters generally means a more capable model, more expensive to run, and slower to respond.

Two warnings. First, parameter count is a poor way to compare models across families, because training data and technique matter at least as much. A well-trained smaller model routinely beats a badly-trained larger one. Second, many providers no longer publish the figure at all, so a confident comparison based on it is often a comparison based on rumour.

### Context window

How much text the model can consider **at once**, measured in tokens. Everything in the window is available to the prediction. Everything outside it does not exist as far as the model is concerned.

The window holds everything: any standing instruction, the whole conversation so far, any document you pasted, and the response being generated. They all compete for the same space.

### The difference in one line

Parameters are what the model **learned, once, permanently**. Context is what the model can **see, right now, temporarily**.

A model with a huge context window and few parameters is like someone with a large desk and little training. A model with many parameters and a small window is like an expert who can only see one page at a time.

### What actually happens when you run out

This is worth knowing precisely, because the failure is quiet.

Some tools return an error saying the input is too long. That is the good case: you know.

Other tools silently drop the oldest part of the conversation to make room. Your standing instruction from twenty messages ago is gone, the model stops following it, and nothing tells you why. If a long conversation starts behaving oddly, this is the first thing to suspect, and the fix is to start fresh and re-state what matters.

## Demonstrate

Measuring your own context use is a genuinely useful habit. Here is how.

```python
# pip install tiktoken
import tiktoken

encoding = tiktoken.get_encoding("cl100k_base")

system_prompt = "You are a careful research assistant. Cite sources."
document = "..." * 2000          # stand-in for something you pasted
question = "Summarise the key findings in five bullet points."

parts = {
    "system prompt": system_prompt,
    "document": document,
    "question": question,
}

total = 0
for name, text in parts.items():
    count = len(encoding.encode(text))
    total += count
    print(f"{name:16} {count:6,} tokens")

print(f"{'total':16} {total:6,} tokens")
```

Run it with a real document you use and the numbers will surprise you. A document that felt short is often most of a budget, and the instruction you care about is a rounding error that gets dropped first.

## Practice

### Exercise: a context budget report

Write a function that takes a dictionary of named text parts and a context limit, and reports how the budget is spent and whether it fits.

```python
import tiktoken


def context_report(parts: dict[str, str], limit: int) -> dict:
    """Report how a context budget is spent across named parts.

    Returns a dict with per-part token counts, the total, the tokens
    remaining, and a boolean saying whether it fits within the limit.
    """
    # Your code here
    ...
```

Expected output for `context_report({"system": "Be brief.", "question": "Why is the sky blue?"}, 100)`:

```
{'parts': {'system': 3, 'question': 6}, 'total': 9, 'remaining': 91, 'fits': True}
```

:::hint Getting started
Build the per-part dictionary first with a comprehension over `parts.items()`, counting each with `len(encoding.encode(text))`. The total is `sum()` of those values. Everything else is arithmetic on the total.
:::

:::solution
```python
import tiktoken


def context_report(parts: dict[str, str], limit: int) -> dict:
    """Report how a context budget is spent across named parts."""
    if limit <= 0:
        raise ValueError("limit must be a positive number of tokens")

    encoding = tiktoken.get_encoding("cl100k_base")
    counts = {name: len(encoding.encode(text)) for name, text in parts.items()}
    total = sum(counts.values())

    return {
        "parts": counts,
        "total": total,
        "remaining": limit - total,
        "fits": total <= limit,
    }


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(context_report({"system": "Be brief.", "question": "Why is the sky blue?"}, 100))
```

Output:

```
{'parts': {'system': 3, 'question': 6}, 'total': 9, 'remaining': 91, 'fits': True}
```

The encoding is created once, outside the comprehension, rather than once per part. That is not premature optimisation: `get_encoding` loads a vocabulary file, and calling it in a loop over a large dictionary is noticeably slow.
:::

### Debugging exercise

This function is meant to report which parts would be dropped, oldest first, if the total exceeds the limit. It has **two** bugs.

```python
def parts_to_drop(counts: dict[str, int], limit: int) -> list[str]:
    total = sum(counts.values())
    dropped = []
    for name, count in counts.items():
        if total < limit:
            return dropped
        dropped.append(name)
        total -= count
    return dropped
```

:::hint What to look at
Trace it with `{"a": 10, "b": 10}` and a limit of 10. What does it return, and what should it return? Then trace it with a total that already fits.
:::

:::solution
**Bug one: the boundary is wrong.** `if total < limit` keeps dropping when the total is exactly at the limit, even though that fits. It should be `total <= limit`.

**Bug two: it checks before subtracting, in the wrong order.** With `{"a": 10, "b": 10}` and a limit of 10, the total is 20. It appends `"a"`, subtracts to 10, then loops: `10 < 10` is false, so it appends `"b"` as well and returns both. It should re-check after each drop, which the corrected boundary handles once the check happens at the right point.

```python
def parts_to_drop(counts: dict[str, int], limit: int) -> list[str]:
    """Names to drop, oldest first, so the remainder fits within limit."""
    total = sum(counts.values())
    dropped = []
    for name, count in counts.items():
        if total <= limit:
            break
        dropped.append(name)
        total -= count
    return dropped
```

With `{"a": 10, "b": 10}` and a limit of 10 this now returns `['a']`, which is correct: dropping `a` leaves 10, which fits.

The first bug is an off-by-one you would probably catch. The second only shows up when the arithmetic happens to land exactly on the boundary, which is the kind of bug that survives casual testing and fails in production.
:::

## What to remember

- Parameters are permanent learned capacity; context is temporary visible text
- Everything competes for the context window: instructions, history, documents, the response
- Running out either errors loudly or drops the oldest text silently
- Odd behaviour late in a long conversation usually means the window overflowed
- Parameter counts are a poor way to compare models, and are often unpublished

lessons.title: Embeddings, explained simply
lessons.description: Turning text into numbers so that similar meanings land close together.
lessons.content:
## Learn

An embedding is a piece of text turned into a list of numbers, in a way that puts **similar meanings close together**.

That is the whole idea, and it is one of the most useful ideas in this course. Module 13 is built entirely on it.

### Why turn text into numbers

Computers compare numbers easily and compare meaning not at all. "The cat sat on the mat" and "A feline rested on the rug" share no words. Any comparison based on matching words says they are unrelated. They plainly are related.

An embedding model reads each sentence and produces a list of numbers -- typically several hundred to a couple of thousand of them. The numbers themselves mean nothing individually. What matters is that the two lists come out **close to each other**, because the sentences mean nearly the same thing.

### Picturing it

Imagine a map where every piece of text is a point.

Texts about cooking cluster in one region. Texts about football cluster in another. Within the cooking region, texts about baking sit closer together than a baking text and a grilling text.

An embedding is the coordinates of a point on that map. Real embeddings have hundreds of dimensions rather than two, which you cannot picture, but nothing about the idea changes -- only the number of coordinates.

### Measuring closeness

The standard measure is **cosine similarity**. It gives a number between -1 and 1:

- Around **1**: the texts point in the same direction, meaning very similar
- Around **0**: unrelated
- Below **0**: rare in practice with modern embedding models, and usually not worth reading much into

In practice you rarely care about the absolute number. You care about ranking: given a question and a thousand paragraphs, which paragraphs are closest? That is a search engine, and it is a much better one than keyword matching because it finds text that means the right thing rather than text that uses the right words.

### What embeddings are not

They are not a summary you can read. You cannot look at the numbers and learn anything.

They are not reversible in any useful way. You cannot reliably reconstruct the original text from the numbers.

And they are not the same as the model's internal representation while generating text. Embedding models are usually separate, smaller models built specifically for this job.

## Demonstrate

The clearest way to see this is to compute it. This example uses `sentence-transformers`, which runs locally and needs no API key.

```python
# pip install sentence-transformers
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer, util

model = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")

query = "How do I reset my password?"
candidates = [
    "Forgot your login details? Use the account recovery link.",
    "Our offices are closed on public holidays.",
    "Password changes take effect immediately across all devices.",
    "The cat sat on the mat.",
]

query_vector = model.encode(query)
candidate_vectors = model.encode(candidates)

scores = util.cos_sim(query_vector, candidate_vectors)[0]

for text, score in sorted(zip(candidates, scores), key=lambda pair: -pair[1]):
    print(f"{score:.3f}  {text}")
```

Expected output, approximately:

```
0.612  Forgot your login details? Use the account recovery link.
0.548  Password changes take effect immediately across all devices.
0.071  Our offices are closed on public holidays.
0.019  The cat sat on the mat.
```

Look at the top result. It shares **not one meaningful word** with the query. No keyword search would have found it. That is the entire value of embeddings, in one line of output.

Your exact numbers will differ by model and version. The ranking is the point, not the decimals.

## Practice

### Exercise: a tiny semantic search

Write a function that takes a query and a list of documents and returns the top matches, each with its score.

```python
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer, util


def search(query: str, documents: list[str], top_k: int = 3) -> list[tuple[str, float]]:
    """Return the top_k documents most similar in meaning to the query.

    Each item is (document, score), sorted from most to least similar.
    """
    # Your code here
    ...
```

Expected shape of the output:

```
[('Forgot your login details? Use the account recovery link.', 0.612),
 ('Password changes take effect immediately across all devices.', 0.548),
 ('Our offices are closed on public holidays.', 0.071)]
```

:::hint Getting started
Encode the query and the documents, compute `util.cos_sim(query_vector, document_vectors)[0]` for a row of scores, pair each score with its document, sort descending, and slice to `top_k`. Convert each score with `float(score)` so you return plain numbers rather than tensors.
:::

:::solution
```python
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer, util

_model = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")


def search(query: str, documents: list[str], top_k: int = 3) -> list[tuple[str, float]]:
    """Return the top_k documents most similar in meaning to the query."""
    if not documents:
        return []

    query_vector = _model.encode(query)
    document_vectors = _model.encode(documents)
    scores = util.cos_sim(query_vector, document_vectors)[0]

    ranked = sorted(
        ((doc, float(score)) for doc, score in zip(documents, scores)),
        key=lambda pair: pair[1],
        reverse=True,
    )
    return ranked[:top_k]


if __name__ == "__main__":
    docs = [
        "Forgot your login details? Use the account recovery link.",
        "Our offices are closed on public holidays.",
        "Password changes take effect immediately across all devices.",
    ]
    for text, score in search("How do I reset my password?", docs):
        print(f"{score:.3f}  {text}")
```

The model is loaded once at module level rather than inside the function. Loading it takes seconds, and doing that on every call would make the function unusable in a loop. The empty-list guard matters too: `model.encode([])` produces an awkward shape that makes `cos_sim` fail with a confusing error.
:::

### Debugging exercise

This function is meant to find the single closest document. It has **two** bugs.

```python
def closest(query: str, documents: list[str]) -> str:
    query_vector = _model.encode(query)
    document_vectors = _model.encode(documents)
    scores = util.cos_sim(query_vector, document_vectors)
    best = min(range(len(documents)), key=lambda i: scores[i])
    return documents[best]
```

:::hint What to look at
Two things. First, what shape does `cos_sim` return when you give it one query and several documents, and what does indexing that shape with a single integer actually get you? Second, on a similarity score, do you want the smallest or the largest?
:::

:::solution
**Bug one: the wrong index into the result.** `util.cos_sim` returns a 2-dimensional result, one row per query. With a single query there is one row, so you need `[0]` to get the row of scores before indexing into it. `scores[i]` is indexing rows, not scores, and will either fail or silently give nonsense.

**Bug two: `min` instead of `max`.** Cosine similarity is higher for more similar text. Taking the minimum returns the **least** similar document -- and it returns it confidently, with no error, which is the dangerous kind of wrong.

```python
def closest(query: str, documents: list[str]) -> str:
    """Return the document closest in meaning to the query."""
    if not documents:
        raise ValueError("documents must not be empty")

    query_vector = _model.encode(query)
    document_vectors = _model.encode(documents)
    scores = util.cos_sim(query_vector, document_vectors)[0]

    best = max(range(len(documents)), key=lambda i: scores[i])
    return documents[best]
```

The second bug is the one worth dwelling on. It produces a plausible-looking answer every time. If your test documents happen to be on unrelated topics you might not notice for a long while, and by then the wrong behaviour is baked into everything built on top.
:::

## What to remember

- An embedding turns text into a list of numbers where similar meanings land close together
- Cosine similarity measures closeness; ranking matters more than the absolute number
- Embeddings find text that means the right thing, not text that uses the right words
- The individual numbers are meaningless and the text cannot be read back out
- This is the foundation of RAG, which is module 13

lessons.title: Transformers and attention
lessons.description: The one idea that made modern language models work.
lessons.content:
## Learn

The transformer is the design that made modern language models work. It was published in 2017, and essentially every model you will use in this course is a variation on it.

You do not need the mathematics. You need one idea.

### The problem it solved

Earlier language models read text **one word at a time, in order**, carrying a summary of everything so far. This had two serious problems.

It was slow, because word 500 could not be processed until words 1 to 499 were done. And it forgot: by the time you reached the end of a long paragraph, the beginning had been compressed into a summary that had lost most of its detail.

### The idea: attention

The transformer reads the whole passage at once, and for every word it works out **which other words matter for understanding this one**.

That is attention. For each word, the model computes a set of weights over all the other words, and builds its representation of that word out of the ones that matter.

### Why this matters, in one example

Take these two sentences:

> The trophy did not fit in the suitcase because **it** was too big.

> The trophy did not fit in the suitcase because **it** was too small.

In the first, "it" means the trophy. In the second, "it" means the suitcase. The sentences differ by one word at the very end, and that word changes what a pronoun near the middle refers to.

An attention mechanism handles this naturally: when processing "it", the model looks at every other word, and "big" versus "small" shifts how much weight goes to "trophy" versus "suitcase". A model reading strictly left to right, carrying a summary, has a much harder time, because the deciding word has not arrived yet.

### Three more things worth knowing

**Attention is computed many times in parallel**, in what are called heads. Different heads end up specialising: some track grammatical relationships, some track which entity a pronoun refers to, some track topic. Nobody assigns these roles; they emerge.

**The layers stack.** Attention happens, the result feeds into the next layer, attention happens again. Dozens of times. Later layers work with representations that already encode a great deal of structure.

**Attention is expensive.** Every word attending to every other word means the cost grows roughly with the square of the length. Double the text and you do around four times the work. This is the main reason context windows have limits and why long inputs cost more, and reducing that cost is an active area of research.

### The honest summary

A transformer reads everything at once, and for every piece of text it decides what else in the passage is relevant to it. Stack that operation many times and you get a system that handles long-range relationships in language far better than anything before it.

That is the level of understanding you need. Everything beyond it is engineering detail that does not change how you use these tools.

## Demonstrate

You can see attention behaving sensibly without touching any mathematics. Take the trophy sentences to any chat tool and ask:

> In "The trophy did not fit in the suitcase because it was too big", what does "it" refer to? Answer in one word.

Then the same with "too small".

You should get "trophy" and "suitcase". The model is not consulting a grammar rule. It is weighting the relationship between words, and one adjective at the end shifts that weighting.

Now try to break it. Construct a sentence where the resolution is genuinely ambiguous to you as a human, and see what the model does. It will still produce a confident answer, because it always does. That is a useful reminder: attention working well on a solvable case does not mean it signals when a case is unsolvable.

## Practice

Write three sentence pairs in the style of the trophy example: identical except for one word, where that word changes what a pronoun refers to.

Test each pair on a chat tool. Record which pairs it handles and which it does not.

Then write two sentences on what you observed. Most people find it handles the clear cases reliably and the genuinely ambiguous ones arbitrarily -- which tells you something about where to be careful when a task turns on the precise reading of a sentence.

## What to remember

- The transformer reads a whole passage at once instead of word by word
- Attention decides, for each word, which other words matter for it
- This handles long-range relationships that earlier designs lost
- Attention heads specialise on their own, without being assigned roles
- The cost grows roughly with the square of the length, which is why context windows have limits

lessons.title: Foundation models
lessons.description: One expensive general model, many cheap specific adaptations.
lessons.content:
## Learn

A foundation model is a single large model, trained once on a broad range of data, that is then adapted to many different tasks.

The name describes its role rather than its architecture. It is the foundation other things are built on.

### The change it represents

Before foundation models, the pattern was one model per task. You wanted sentiment analysis, so you collected labelled examples of sentiment and trained a sentiment model. You wanted translation, so you did it again, from scratch, with a different dataset.

Every task meant a new dataset, a new training run, and a new model that could do exactly one thing.

The foundation model pattern inverts this. Train one very large model on a very broad range of data. Then adapt it, cheaply, to whatever you need -- often by simply describing the task in a prompt.

That word "cheaply" is doing a lot of work. Building the foundation model is extraordinarily expensive and only a handful of organisations do it. Adapting one is something you can do in an afternoon, and it is what most of this course is about.

### Three ways to adapt one

In rough order of cost:

**Prompting.** Describe the task in the input. Free, instant, and by far the most common. This is module 4.

**Retrieval.** Give the model relevant documents alongside the question. Moderate effort, no training. This is module 13.

**Fine-tuning.** Train the model further on your own examples. Real cost and real expertise, and mostly used when the first two genuinely are not enough.

The important practical point: most people reach for fine-tuning far too early. Prompting and retrieval solve the large majority of problems, and they are reversible in a way that fine-tuning is not.

### Why it is not only language

The same pattern appears across the field. Image models trained broadly are adapted to specific visual tasks. Audio models trained on large amounts of speech are adapted to particular languages or voices. Multimodal foundation models handle several kinds of input at once.

The shape is always the same: one expensive general model, many cheap specific adaptations.

### The part that should give you pause

Everything built on a foundation model inherits its properties. Its biases. Its knowledge cutoff. Its failure modes. Its blind spots.

If thousands of applications are built on a handful of foundation models, then a flaw in one of those models is not an isolated problem -- it propagates everywhere at once. This concentration is a genuine concern in the field, and it is worth holding onto as you build things in later modules.

## Demonstrate

Here is the pattern made concrete. One model, five tasks, no training, only different prompts.

Take any chat tool and run these in sequence, each in a fresh conversation:

1. *"Classify the sentiment of this review as positive, negative or mixed: 'Arrived late but the quality is excellent.'"*
2. *"Translate into French: 'The meeting has been moved to Thursday.'"*
3. *"Extract every date mentioned in this text, as a list: ..."*
4. *"Write a Python function that checks whether a string is a palindrome."*
5. *"Summarise the following in exactly two sentences: ..."*

Five tasks that, a decade ago, would have been five separate research projects with five separate datasets. Same model, five prompts, a few minutes.

That is the foundation model pattern, and seeing it in one sitting is worth more than any amount of explanation.

## Practice

Think of a task specific to your own field, study or work -- something a general-purpose tool would not have been built for.

Write a prompt that describes the task clearly enough for a model to attempt it, and try it. Some examples: classify support tickets into your team's own categories; rewrite a paragraph into your organisation's house style; extract the structured fields your department cares about from a document.

Record how well it did on a first attempt with no examples. Keep this; you will improve the same prompt substantially in module 4, and the comparison is instructive.

## What to remember

- A foundation model is one broadly trained model adapted to many tasks
- It replaced the pattern of one purpose-built model per task
- Adaptation is by prompting, retrieval, or fine-tuning, in increasing order of cost
- Most problems are solved by the first two, and fine-tuning is usually reached for too early
- Everything built on a foundation model inherits its biases and failure modes

lessons.title: Practice questions and answer key
lessons.description: Ten questions covering the whole module, with a full explanation for each.
lessons.content:
These questions cover the whole of module 2. Answer before you check, and read the explanation for each one, including the questions you get right.

:::quiz
Q. What is a neural network, described as plainly as possible?
- A simulation of how brain cells work
+ A very large mathematical function: numbers in, numbers out, arithmetic in between
- A database of facts with a search layer on top
- A set of rules written by engineers and refined over time
= It is arithmetic at enormous scale. The word "neural" comes from a loose analogy that has caused a lot of confusion; nothing about these systems should be reasoned about by thinking about brains.

Q. A language model is fundamentally trained to do what?
- Answer questions accurately
- Understand the meaning of a sentence
+ Predict what text comes next
- Retrieve the most relevant stored fact
= Next-token prediction is the whole training objective. Question answering, translation, summarising and coding are all that one ability applied in different situations, which is why the same model can do tasks nobody trained it for.

Q. You correct a model's mistake and it agrees with you. What has changed about the model?
- It has updated the relevant weights
- It has stored a correction for future conversations
+ Nothing at all
- It has flagged the topic for review during the next training run
= Training and inference are separate. During inference the weights are frozen. The model produced a likely continuation of a conversation in which someone was corrected. Open a new conversation and the same mistake is available again.

Q. A long conversation starts ignoring an instruction you gave at the beginning. What is the most likely cause?
- The model has been updated mid-conversation
+ The conversation exceeded the context window and the earliest text was dropped
- The instruction was ambiguous
- The model is refusing the instruction
= Everything competes for the same context window: instructions, history, pasted documents and the response. When it overflows, some tools error and others silently drop the oldest text. Odd behaviour late in a long conversation should make you suspect this first.

Q. What is the practical difference between parameters and the context window?
- Parameters are for text, the context window is for images
+ Parameters are permanent learned capacity; the context window is temporary visible text
- Parameters are set by the user, the context window by the provider
- They are two names for the same measurement
= Parameters are what the model learned once, during training, and they never change while you use it. The context window is what it can see right now, and it is emptied every conversation.

Q. Two sentences share no words but mean nearly the same thing. What puts them close together?
- Tokenization
+ Their embeddings
- The attention mechanism
- Their parameter counts
= An embedding maps text to numbers such that similar meanings land near each other. This is why semantic search finds text that means the right thing rather than text that uses the right words, and it is the foundation of RAG in module 13.

Q. What does the attention mechanism in a transformer actually do?
- It decides which parts of the training data to memorise
+ For each piece of text, it works out which other parts of the passage are relevant to it
- It focuses the model on the user's most recent message
- It filters out irrelevant words before processing
= Attention computes, for every position, a weighting over all other positions. This is what lets a model resolve a pronoun using a word that appears much later, which earlier designs that read strictly left to right handled badly.

Q. Why do longer inputs cost disproportionately more?
- Longer inputs use more parameters
+ Attention compares every position with every other, so cost grows roughly with the square of the length
- Longer inputs require more training
- Tokenization becomes less efficient on long text
= Doubling the length means roughly four times the attention work. This is the main reason context windows have limits and why long documents get expensive, and reducing that cost is an active research area.

Q. Your team wants a model to always follow a detailed internal style guide. What should you try first?
- Fine-tune a model on your organisation's documents
+ Put the style guide in the prompt, via a standing instruction or system prompt
- Train a model from scratch on your house style
- Ask the model to memorise the guide at the start of each conversation
= Prompting is free, instant and reversible, and it solves most problems of this shape. Fine-tuning is real cost and real expertise, and it is routinely reached for far too early. Asking a model to memorise something does nothing, because it cannot.

Q. What is the main risk of a great many applications being built on a handful of foundation models?
- The models become too expensive to run
+ Every application inherits the same biases, cutoffs and failure modes
- Applications become too similar to one another
- Fine-tuning stops being possible
= Anything built on a foundation model inherits its properties. A flaw in a widely-used model is not an isolated problem; it propagates into everything built on top of it at once. This concentration is a genuine concern in the field.
:::

## How to read your score

Seven or more means you are ready for module 3. Fewer than seven, go back to the lesson covering what you missed. Module 3 leans on tokens, context windows and hallucination in particular.

lessons.title: Hands-on lab: measuring tokens, context and similarity
lessons.description: Forty minutes measuring this module's three ideas on your own text.
lessons.content:
This lab takes about forty minutes. You will measure the three things this module described -- tokens, context and similarity -- on text of your own, so the numbers stop being abstract.

## Before you start

You need Python and two packages:

```bash
pip install tiktoken sentence-transformers
```

`sentence-transformers` downloads a model the first time you run it, which takes a minute or two. Neither package needs an API key or an account.

Have a real document to hand: an essay, a report, a set of lecture notes, a long email thread. Something you actually wrote or read, at least a few hundred words.

## Step 1: Tokens against intuition

Before measuring, write down your guess for how many tokens your document is.

Then measure it:

```python
import tiktoken

encoding = tiktoken.get_encoding("cl100k_base")
text = open("your_document.txt", encoding="utf-8").read()

words = len(text.split())
tokens = len(encoding.encode(text))

print(f"characters: {len(text):,}")
print(f"words:      {words:,}")
print(f"tokens:     {tokens:,}")
print(f"tokens per word: {tokens / words:.2f}")
```

Record all four numbers and how far off your guess was. Most people underestimate.

## Step 2: Where the tokens go

Not all text tokenizes equally. Find out what is expensive in yours.

Split your document into paragraphs and print the token count of each. Then find the five most token-dense paragraphs per word. Look at what they have in common -- usually numbers, code, unusual names, URLs, or non-English text.

```python
paragraphs = [p for p in text.split("\n\n") if p.strip()]

dense = sorted(
    ((len(encoding.encode(p)) / max(len(p.split()), 1), p) for p in paragraphs),
    reverse=True,
)[:5]

for ratio, paragraph in dense:
    print(f"{ratio:.2f} tokens/word: {paragraph[:80]}...")
```

Record what the dense paragraphs have in common.

## Step 3: A context budget

Pick a real context limit -- use 8,000 tokens if you have nothing specific in mind -- and work out what fits.

Using the `context_report` function you wrote in the parameters lesson, or writing it again here, report the budget for: a system instruction of your choosing, your document, and a question about it.

Then answer, in writing: does it fit? If not, what would you cut, and what would you lose by cutting it?

## Step 4: Similarity on your own text

Take five sentences from your document. Write a question that one of them answers.

Run the semantic search from the embeddings lesson against those five sentences.

Record: did the right sentence come top? What was its score, and what was the runner-up? Was there a sentence you expected to rank higher than it did?

## Step 5: Break it deliberately

Now find a case where similarity gets it wrong.

Write a question whose answer is in your document but phrased very differently, with no overlapping vocabulary. See whether the embedding still finds it.

Then write a question that uses a lot of the same words as an irrelevant sentence, and see whether that sentence wrongly comes top.

:::hint I cannot construct a failing case
Try negation. "The deadline was extended" and "The deadline was not extended" are near-identical in embedding space and opposite in meaning. Embeddings are notoriously weak on negation, and it is one of the most useful failure modes to have seen for yourself before you rely on retrieval in module 13.
:::

## Step 6: Write it up

Five short paragraphs, three hundred words or so:

1. Your token guess versus the real count, and what made the difference
2. What kind of text turned out to be token-expensive in your document
3. Whether your document fits a realistic context budget, and what you would cut
4. Whether semantic search found the right sentence, with the actual scores
5. The failing case you constructed, and what it tells you about when not to trust similarity

## What good looks like

A strong write-up has **numbers in it**. "The document was longer than I thought" is weak. "I guessed 800 tokens, it was 1,340, because the tables of figures cost about 2.1 tokens per word against 1.3 for the prose" is strong.

A strong write-up is also specific about step 5. Everyone can run the happy path. Finding a case where the technique fails, and saying what it implies, is the part that will matter when you build something in module 13.

lessons.title: Assignment: explain a model to a non-technical audience
lessons.description: Explain an LLM to a named person, marked against a published rubric.
lessons.content:
## The task

Explain how a large language model works to a specific non-technical person, in a form they would actually read.

This is harder than it sounds, and it is the best possible test of whether you understood this module. You cannot hide behind terminology. If you do not understand attention, it will show the moment you try to explain it without the word.

## Choose your audience first

Name a real person or a specific group, and write for them. Some that work well:

- A parent or grandparent who has heard about AI on the news and is uneasy about it
- A manager who has to decide whether the team should use these tools
- A humanities undergraduate who is curious but has avoided anything technical
- A school student aged about fifteen
- A small business owner deciding whether to pay for a subscription

Name them at the top of your submission. The rest of the piece is marked against whether it suits that audience.

## What to submit

One piece of writing, **seven hundred to a thousand words**, covering all six of these. The order is yours; the list is not.

1. **What the model is.** Weights, arithmetic, scale. No brain analogy.
2. **What it was trained to do.** Next-token prediction, and why that produces so much more than it sounds like it should.
3. **Training versus inference.** Specifically that it does not learn from your conversation.
4. **The context window.** What it is, and what running out of it looks like from the user's side.
5. **Why it makes things up.** Connect hallucination to next-token prediction. This is the section that matters most.
6. **One thing your audience should do differently** having read this.

Plus, at the end and outside the word count, a short note on **where you used AI in writing this and what you changed**.

## Constraints

**No jargon without a plain-English definition in the same sentence.** You may use the word "token" if you say what one is where you first use it. The same for parameters, context window, inference.

**At least two concrete analogies**, and neither may be the brain.

**One worked example** the reader can follow, or better, try themselves.

**No claim you have not verified.** If you state a number, say where it came from. This is a module about a system that invents confident facts; inventing one in an essay about it would be an unfortunate way to lose marks.

## Rubric

Marked out of 100.

**Audience fit, 20 marks.** Full marks where the vocabulary, examples and length genuinely suit the named person and the piece would survive contact with them. Half marks for a generic "non-technical reader" piece. Few marks where the audience is named but the writing ignores them.

**Technical accuracy, 25 marks.** Full marks where all six required points are correct and nothing is oversimplified into being wrong. The most common way to lose marks here is implying the model understands, remembers, or looks things up.

**Explaining hallucination, 20 marks.** Full marks where the reader could explain, afterwards, *why* a model invents things -- connected to next-token prediction, not presented as a bug someone forgot to fix. This section carries heavy weight because it is the single most useful thing a non-technical person can learn about these tools.

**Analogies and the worked example, 20 marks.** Full marks for two analogies that genuinely illuminate and do not mislead, plus an example the reader could follow. Marks are lost for analogies that create a new misconception, which brain analogies almost always do.

**Clarity and honesty, 15 marks.** Full marks for prose your audience would read willingly, with every term defined, every claim verified, and the AI-use note present and specific. Marks are lost for jargon left undefined and for unverified numbers.

## What will cost you marks

**Any version of "it thinks" or "it understands".** These are the exact misconceptions the piece exists to prevent. If you need a verb, "produces", "predicts" and "generates" all work.

**Explaining the transformer architecture in detail.** Your audience does not need it and will stop reading. The idea of attention, in one sentence, is enough.

**Being so careful that it becomes useless.** A piece hedged into meaninglessness fails the audience just as badly as one that overclaims. Your reader should finish with a clear, correct, usable mental model, not a list of caveats.

:::hint I do not know how to explain attention without the jargon
Use the trophy sentence. "The trophy did not fit in the suitcase because it was too big" versus "too small". Ask your reader which thing "it" refers to in each. They will get it instantly, and they will also see that the deciding word comes after the word it decides. Then: the model works out, for every word, which other words matter for it. That is attention, and you never had to say "attention head" or draw a diagram.
:::
